remain short-lived. Thus, diminishing risks linked with long-execution Lambdas, 
such as unanticipated crashes that could compromise data integrity. This 
approach aligns with the AWS serverless model guidelines, where functions are 
idempotent, event-triggered, and automatically scale (AWS, n.d.). 
The decision to use ECS for user-request handling was to prioritise user wait 
times, as highlighted in the Non-Functional Requirements. The ECS will only 
handle requests originating directly from the user, whereas all other events 
should be handled by serverless options such as Lambdas to reduce costs. The 
choice of ECS a serverless Lambda is to mitigate latencies arising from cold 
starts. 
The newUser Lambda function is trigged upon account validation and will create 
a new entry within the userStats table. This again follows the event driven 
architecture principle, making the solution highly scalable and the code cleaner 
(AWS, n.d.). While the use of DynamoDB tables ensures that data is encrypted 
and is backed up, encase of system failure. 
Using Route53 in conjunction with a certificate manage, enables for a custom 
HTTPS domain, following industry best practices ensuring that data transmission 
remains secure. 
Finally, placing services within a private VPC subnet while publicly exposing the 
Elastic Load Balancer and Cognito, follows the security principle of least privilege 
(AWS, n.d.). This strategy limits the exposure of services to the internet, 
ensuring that other services remain only indirectly accessible, thus improving 
the clouds security. It is worth noting within the actual implementation of the 
project none of resources, except for the ECS, were within a VPC due to high 
costs; however, if the project was to be released to the public there would only 
need to be minor changed made to the IaC to enable it.
